blocks.text: [II, 565] See the traces of this story in the Chaldaica of Abydenus, cited by Eusebius, book 9 of the Praeparatio, and by Cyril in the first book against Julian: Τρίτη δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ἔπειτα ὑὼν ἐκόπασε, μεθίει τῶν ὀρνίθων πείρην ποιούμενος, εἴπου γῆν ἴδοι, τοῦ ὕδατος ἐκδῦσαν. αἱ δὲ ἐκδεχομένου σφέας πελάγεος ἀχανέος, ἀπορέουσαι ὅπη καθορμίσονται, παρὰ τὸν Ξίσουθρον ὀπίσω κομίζονται, καὶ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇσιν ἕτεραι, ὡς δὲ τῇσι τρίτησιν εὐτύχεεν· ἀφίκατο γὰρ δὴ πηλοῦ κατάπλεοι τοὺς ταρσοὺς, θεοί μιν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀφανίζουσιν [Tritē de hēmera epeita hyōn ekopase, methiei tōn ornithōn peirēn poioumenos, eipou gēn idoi, tou hydatos ekdysan. hai de ekdechomenou spheas pelageos achaneos, aporeousai hopē kathormisontai, para ton Xisouthron opisō komizontai, kai ep᾽ autēsin heterai, hōs de tēsi tritēsin eutycheen; aphikato gar dē pēlou katapleoi tous tarsous, theoi min ex anthrōpōn aphanizousin], On the third day after it had stopped raining, he (Xisuthrus, as he calls Noah) sent out some birds to make a trial, whether he might see land emerging from the water. But since the boundless sea everywhere received them, and they were uncertain where to land, they came back to him; and after these, others. When he succeeded with the third ones sent out, for they had returned with muddy feet, the gods removed him from among men. He says birds in the plural, because Noah sent out a raven and a dove. And that they returned muddy, just as Eutychius also says of the dove, p. 40: رجعت رجلتها مبلولة بالماء [rajaʿat rijlatuhā mablūla bi-l-māʾ] It returned with its feet wet with water. And before him Josephus: ὑπανελθούσης δὲ πεπηλομένης [hypanelthousēs de pepēlomenēs], but when it had returned muddy. For in Hebrew we have ותבא אליו היונה, and the dove came back to him. And יון, which means mud, alludes to the name of the dove, יונה. Finally, what was said of the birds, or at least of the dove, that it flew away and did not return, Abydenus ineptly transferred to Xisuthrus, or Noah, as if he had then been removed from the midst. But the Greeks report this very thing in such a way that you would hardly find anything lacking in them, except that they substitute their own Deucalion for Noah. Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Οἱ μὲν οὖν μυθολόγοι τῷ Δευκαλίωνί φασι περιστερὰν ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ ἀποπτᾶσαν [Hoi men oun mythologoi tō Deukalioni phasi peristeran ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de apoptasan]. The mythographers say that a dove, sent out of the ark, signalled a storm to Deucalion when it came back inside, and fair weather when it flew away. The Arab dream-interpreters attribute to the ورشان [warashān] vvarsen, that is, the wood pigeon, what Moses attributes to the dove. For thus they say of the wood pigeon in Damir, in the chapter الورشان [al-warashān] Alvvarsen: وهو في المنام رجل غريب يدل علي اخبار ورسل لانه اخبر توحا عليه [col. 32] السلام تنقص الما لما كان في السفينة [wa-huwa fī l-manām rajul gharīb yadullu ʿalā akhbār wa-rusul li-annahu akhbara Tūḥan ʿalayhi al-salām tanaqquṣ al-mā lammā kāna fī l-safīna] Seen in sleep by a stranger, it signifies messengers and couriers, because it announced to Noah, peace be upon him, when he was in the ark, the decrease of the waters. The Arabs, namely, prefer the wood pigeon to the dove because God is believed to have appeared to Muhammad in the form of a wood pigeon and to have inspired many things. Ludovico di Varthema, Navigation, book 1, ch. 18: While we were on our way (towards Mecca) countless wood pigeons darkened the sky. They say that birds of this kind descend from that bird which spoke into the ear of Muhammad under the guise of the Holy Spirit. See the rest there.

[II, 566] So much for the literal sense of the story of the dove which Noah sent out of the ark. As for the mystical sense, many hold that the olive leaf, or twig, was a symbol of the peace and covenant which God was shortly to make with Noah. Tertullian, On Baptism, book 8: After the baptism (so to speak) of the world, the dove, herald of heaven's wrath appeased, announced peace to the earth, sent out of the ark and returning with the olive, a sign which is held out for peace among the nations too. Jerome, Epist. 83 to Oceanus, ch. 3: With a branch of refreshment and light it announces peace to the world. And in the Dialogue against Lucifer: The dove announces peace to the earth. Chrysostom on Matthew, Homily 12: Κλάδον φέρον ἐλαίας, τὴν κοινὴν τῆς οἰκουμένης γαλήνην εὐηγγελίσατο [Kladon pheron elaias, tēn koinēn tēs oikoumenēs galēnēn euēngelisato]; Bearing an olive branch, it proclaimed the common calm of the world. Amoenus in the Enchiridion of the Old and New Testament:

Messenger of the flood now abating, the dove brings back to the ark in its beak a branch of the green olive: for the raven, caught by gluttony among foul carcasses, had stayed; she brings back the new joys of peace granted.
— — — sent out again, she brings back a small offering of the peace-bearing fruit of the olive.
And seeing the peace-bearing branch of the green olive, she plucks it and carries it back in her gentle beak to those shut in.
For the olive is a sign of peace. Virgil, book 2 of the Georgics:
He orders a hundred envoys to go to the king's narrow walls, all veiled with branches of Pallas.
And in his hand he holds out a branch of the peace-bearing olive,
Veiled with olive branches, and begging for pardon.
